newsitem.title: USA: Job fear effect on prices temporary--SF Fed expert.
newsitem.headline: Job fear effect on prices temporary--SF Fed expert.

text.p: The current strength of U.S. labor markets suggests any wage-moderating effect on inflation is likely to be temporary, a Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco economist said.
"On that issue, I largely agree with (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan," Robert Valletta, a labor market economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, told Reuters.
"What Mr. Greenspan pointed out (during his recent Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress) is that he feels this is likely to be a temporary factor," the economist said.
Valletta said Greenspan's recent congressional remarks indicated the chairman felt job insecurity was the key factor holding down wage and, therefore, price inflation in 1996.

"Although he (Greenspan) did not make a specific prediction about when this factor is going to end, he noted that there is substantial risk that it could end at some point soon during 1997," Valletta said.
"When that happens, we're likely to start seeing an uptick in wage and price inflation," the Fed economist said.

U.S. labor markets have been tight for several months, with the latest employment report compiled by the Labor Department showing a jobless rate of 5.3 percent in February with a healthy 339,000 job gain in non-farm payrolls.

However, no inflation-threatening increase in wages has been detected yet. The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI), for example, has been between an annualized rate of 2.0 and 3.0 percent for many months now.
However, recent comments from some key figures at the Federal Reserve hinted at how alert central bank officials are about any signs of inflation.

President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Michael Moskow said on Thursday the Fed sees wages rising, but not labor costs in general. He added, however, the central bank cannot allow inflation to heat up even "a little bit."
Also on Thursday, Federal Reserve Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin said the Fed needs to be especially vigilant for any threat of faster inflation.
The discussion has gained momentum over the last few weeks as the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) March 25 meeting looms.
Several Wall Street pundits believe the Fed is likely to raise short-term interest rates at the March meeting as a pre-emptive strike against future inflation.
In a recent Reuters survey, 17 of 35 U.S. primary dealers expected the Fed to raise rates on March 25.
If such predictions are confirmed, it will be the first time in almost two years the Fed has raised its target for the federal funds rate, which is currently at 5.25 percent.
Some analysts said, however, the March meeting might be too soon for the Fed to move.

Former Fed Vice Chairman Preston Martin said labor markets have changed in this decade, requiring a new analytical approach. He also said he believes the economy is weaker than the latest government data indicate.
"This economy is weaker than the BLS (Bureau of Labor Statistics) ... data would lead us to believe," said Martin, who is currently the chairman of Home Vest Financial Services.
"Yes, be pre-emptive (when it comes to inflation) ... but don't pre-empt too soon," the former Fed vice chairman said.
Martin, who served when Paul Volcker was Fed chairman in the 1980s, said he would vote for no change in policy at the March meeting if he were still on the FOMC.
